svg.title: The paired 2x2 table and McNemar's test on the 9 discordant items
svg.desc: Model A scores 41 of 50 correct (82.0%) and Model B scores 42 of 50 correct (84.0%) on the same 50-item set, a headline gap of plus 2.0 points. The paired 2x2 table has four cells: both correct = 37, A correct and B wrong = 4, A wrong and B correct = 5, both wrong = 4, summing to 50. Only the 9 discordant items (the 4 where A alone was right plus the 5 where B alone was right) carry any signal about which model is better; the 41 concordant items are uninformative. McNemar's test treats those 9 disagreements as coin flips: the uncorrected chi-square is (4 minus 5) squared over 9, equal to 0.111; the Yates-corrected chi-square is 0.000; the chi-square approximation gives p equal to 0.739; the exact two-sided binomial p-value, 2 times the sum of C(9,0) through C(9,4) which is 256, divided by 2 to the 9th power which is 512, equals 1.000. A 5-versus-4 split of 9 coin flips is exactly what chance looks like, so the plus 2 point gap is not statistically significant on this set. A power panel shows that reliably detecting a true 2 point gain at 80% power needs about 5528 items per model unpaired, or about 3515 items total when paired, far more than the 50-item set used here.
